title: Orbital Rhabdomyosarcoma: A Pediatric Emergency
summary: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common primary orbital malignancy in children, characterized by its rapid, alarming progression. Early diagnosis via urgent biopsy and multi-modal treatment with chemotherapy and radiotherapy has transformed this once-fatal disease into one with a high survival rate.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Orbital Rhabdomyosarcoma is a highly malignant neoplasm of primitive mesenchymal cells that show a tendency toward rhabdomyoblastic differentiation. Despite its name, it does not typically arise from extraocular muscles but from undifferentiated pluripotent cells. It is a true ophthalmic emergency due to its potential for rapid orbital expansion and intracranial spread.

sections.title: Clinical Features: The Rapid Onset
content: Sudden, rapidly progressive proptosis (days to weeks)
Globe displacement (usually downward/outward for Embryonal)
Ptosis and lid edema with characteristic discoloration
Palpable, non-tender, firm orbital mass
Decreased ocular motility (ophthalmoplegia)
Pain is rare (only 10%), mimicking cellulitis
Late findings: Optic disc edema, choroidal folds

rows: Fever, leukocytosis, paranasal sinus opacification on CT, pain with movement.
Often bilateral, ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), adrenal primary on imaging.
Usually present at birth/infancy, blanches with pressure, Valsalva increase.
Acute onset only if hemorrhage occurs ('chocolate cyst'), slow growth otherwise.
Pain is a hallmark, dramatic response to corticosteroids.
Associated with AML, requires peripheral blood smear/marrow biopsy.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Urgent Imaging: CT (bone destruction) and MRI (soft tissue detail, T2 hyperintense).
2. Urgent Incisional Biopsy: Gold standard; avoid complete excision if it risks vital structures.
3. Immunohistochemistry: Test for Desmin, Myogenin, MyoD1, and Muscle-specific Actin.
4. Systemic Staging: Chest CT, Bone Scan, Bone Marrow Aspiration, and Lumbar Puncture (for parameningeal).
5. Pre-treatment Labs: CBC, LFTs, Renal function (baseline for chemotherapy).

rows: Incomplete resection or biopsy only (Most common)

sections.title: Management Strategy (IRS Protocols)
content: Step 1: Biopsy to confirm diagnosis and subtype.
Step 2: Debulking surgery only if vision/nerves are not compromised.
Step 3: Chemotherapy (VAC Regime) for 6–12 months.
Step 4: Radiotherapy (External Beam) for Groups II, III, and IV.
Step 5: Orbital Exenteration (Reserved for resistant or recurrent cases).

sections.title: The 'VAC' Chemotherapy Regimen
content: Vincristine: Mitotic inhibitor (microtubule disruption).
Actinomycin D (Dactinomycin): RNA synthesis inhibitor.
Cyclophosphamide: Alkylating agent (DNA cross-linking).
Orbital RMS is exquisitely chemosensitive.

sections.title: EMERGENCY: RED FLAGS
content: Rapidly increasing proptosis over 24-48 hours
New onset ophthalmoplegia in a child
Evidence of bony erosion on CT scan
Presence of 'raccoon eyes' (suggests metastatic neuroblastoma or RMS)
Distant metastases to lungs or bone (check for respiratory distress or bone pain)

content.explanation: To confirm RMS, remember the M's: Myogenin (most specific), MyoD1 (very sensitive), and Muscle-Specific Actin (MSA). These confirm the cell is trying to become a muscle cell.

sections.title: Surgical Principles
content: Primary goal: Tissue for diagnosis and IHC.
Avoid Exenteration as primary therapy (no survival benefit over chemo/RT).
Incisional biopsy is preferred over fine-needle aspiration (FNA) for architecture.
Lid-sparing approaches where possible.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Boards
content: Embryonal is 'Everyone' (most common) and occurs 'Everywhere' (but favors superonasal).
Alveolar is 'Awful' (worse prognosis) and occurs 'At the bottom' (inferior orbit).
RMS is the most common pediatric orbital primary, but Metastatic Neuroblastoma is the most common pediatric orbital secondary.
Cross-striations on H&E are found in only ~50-60% of cases; IHC is necessary.
Radiation doses are typically 40-50 Gy, but can cause late complications like cataract, dry eye, and orbital hypoplasia.

sections.title: Complications & Long-term Follow-up
content: Radiation-induced cataract (near 100% within years).
Radiation keratopathy and severe xerophthalmia.
Orbital bone growth arrest (facial asymmetry).
Secondary malignancies (Osteosarcoma) in the radiation field.
Infertility or secondary leukemia from alkylating agents (Cyclophosphamide).

sections.title: Landmark Studies: IRS I to IV
sections.content: The Intergroup Rhabdomyosarcoma Studies (IRS) have shown that orbital RMS has a 'favorable site' prognosis. IRS-IV established that pulsed VAC chemotherapy is highly effective and that local control is best achieved with 45-50.4 Gy radiation for residual disease. Current COG (Children's Oncology Group) trials aim to reduce toxicity by lowering radiation doses in specific 'low-risk' embryonal cohorts.
